#5263. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

#5261. ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and issues shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration shows how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 new shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS says the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets quickly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a plan as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For users, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

Binance will delist five crypto spot trading pairs within the next 24 hours on Nov. 20, 2026, following a review.

To protect its users and to ensure a high-quality trading market, Binance conducts regular reviews of all listed spot trading pairs; it may delist certain spot trading pairs for various reasons, including low liquidity and trading volume.

Binance will delist GAS/TRY, HBAR/BNB, HIVE/TRY, KSM/TRY and ZAMA/TRY pairs on November 20, 2026 at 03:00 UTC, according to an official announcement published on November 18.

Four of the five affected pairs are related to the Turkish lira (TRY), while the last one is HBAR/BNB. The decision affects trading between these specific assets and does not mean the cryptocurrencies themselves are being completely delisted from Binance.

The exchange clarified that users will still be able to trade the affected tokens through other available spot trading pairs on its platform.

Binance will terminate Spot Trading Bots services for the spot trading pairs simultaneously where applicable. Users are strongly advised to update and/or cancel their Spot Trading Bots prior to the cessation of services for Spot Trading Bots to avoid any potential losses.

In related news, Binance Margin will initiate a routine cleanup of Cross Margin accounts with collateral valued at less than 1 USD (or equivalent in other assets), effective from November 30, 2026 at 00:00 (UTC). The cleanup will be executed on a daily basis as an ongoing operational process.

Affected accounts include Cross Margin Accounts with a collateral value of less than 1 USD equivalent across all assets and no outstanding liabilities, as well as Margin Accounts with no capital activity in the past 6 months. Capital activity refers to any action that generates a capital flow.

For each eligible Small-Asset Account, the system will automatically transfer the collateral in users’ Margin Accounts to their Spot Accounts while the Margin Account functions remain normal, allowing users to transfer, borrow, or trade at any time after the cleanup.

Accounts with collateral equal to or exceeding 1 USD equivalent are not affected by this cleanup.

#5258. Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

Behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

The Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab says it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card shows 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

Elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each new token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

The vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

This release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

#5257. Italian Banking Giant Rotates Crypto ETF Portfolio From Bitcoin to Solana and XRP

Italy’s largest banking group, Intesa Sanpaolo, increased its spot altcoin ETF holdings according to a new disclosure. This follows capital rotation out of Bitcoin products by a slew of traditional firms amid dwindling market sentiment.

The bank’s disclosed crypto ETF holdings grew in Q3 2026 to $108.56 million, up $17 million, while digital asset prices moved sideways. In June, total assets were worth $90 million as it looked to diversify and grow holdings systematically.

Bitcoin, the largest asset in the portfolio, was reduced to make room for altcoins in a possible bid to diversify assets. At the end of Q2, BTC holdings stood at $69.32 million but dropped slightly to above $61 million last quarter. The firm’s Ethereum exposure also dropped to $5 million.

However, Solana and XRP products filled the vacuum, highlighting institutional appetite for these assets. At the time of writing, the bank’s spot Solana ETF exposure is at $14.1 million after its investment in the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF ballooned from seven shares to 875,407 shares.

Intesa’s XRP investment also grew over the same period to $27.2 million, driven mainly by 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF. The company’s shares in the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF remained unchanged across both quarters.

More broadly, the bank reduced its Bitcoin ETF exposure and increased SOL and XRP products. Most experts believe it follows the current market trend, and firms, especially traditional companies, need to diversify to make up for Bitcoin’s decline.

Historically, during bear phases, there’s a huge rotation of capital into altcoins, though it’s not sustained for long. As expected, Solana and XRP become institutional favorites, while Ethereum trades similarly to Bitcoin.

The former have the potential to record spikes within the red wave, like in 2022 before the approval of spot ETF products in the United States. These products opened up digital assets to a new stash of traditional capital.

Intesa and other banks have since increased their crypto exposure, driven by the need to diversify assets and a broader adoption spree. Heightened institutional and retail interests pushed Bitcoin to an all-time high above $125k last year. Currently, BTC trades at $63,819, while Ethereum is slightly below $1,800.

#5255. Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

The reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery plan has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

SlowMist's finding is precise: the withdrawal function released assets without independently verifying the actual event on the source chain. A signature confirmed that the signer approved a message. It did not confirm that the message matched a deposit that existed, that was still unused, and that involved the same recipient, token and amount.The replay angle deserves attention, even though SlowMist's summary only implies it. A bridge normally marks each source event as consumed, keyed to something fixed like the source chain, transaction hash and log index, so it can be paid out once. If replay protection keys on the contents of the receipt instead, changing the recipient, token or amount produces a receipt the contract has never seen. Five edited receipts against one deposit would then look like five fresh claims. That is one plausible way the pieces fit together, not a finding the researchers have published.Bridge history offers parallels. In 2022, Wormhole lost about $325 million when an attacker got a forged message past its signature verification, and Nomad lost about $190 million after a misconfiguration let nearly any message pass as valid. The Ankr case is smaller, but it shares the same root: the verification step accepted something it shouldn't have.

The Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most important fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

The lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Users with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its plan for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

#5254. What’s Coming for Solana in 2027? Upgrade Planned Across Four Key Areas

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

At the 2026 Breakpoint event, Brennan Watt, CEO of Anza, gave a walkthrough of Solana’s wins this year, while sharing what is in store for 2027.

According to Watt, 2026 was a major year for Solana as it migrated its consensus to Alpenglow, slashed the block times in half from 400 ms to 200 ms while doubling capacity.

The Alpenglow upgrade went live on mainnet on October 21, 2026, cutting transaction finality from about 12.8 seconds down to roughly 150 milliseconds. It replaced TowerBFT with Votor, a faster path to reaching agreement.

After Alpenglow, @bw_solana laid out @anza_xyz roadmap for Solana in 2027 Performance: network compute capacity doubles, transactions cut 80% CU units for token accounts Expressivity: vector processing for models running fully onchain, 64 → 96 accounts per transaction, read account data instead of copying it so less data moves per transaction Market Structure: Alpenglow. Next with faster block distribution and Constellation for clearer ordering rules and more competition among validators Resilience: simpler protocol with fewer special cases, safer to change https://t.co/EpvDdSyjln

Solana recently transitioned to 1.0, marking the network’s graduation from “mainnet beta” to “mainnet” and retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch. Solana 1.0 recognizes the progress on network performance, resilience, and developer experience.

According to Watt, Solana is eyeing significant improvements in 2027 across four categories. First is Resilience, which involves simplifying the protocol, reducing special cases, and making it safer to change.

“So, we're going to go ahead and simplify the protocol, replacing legacy abstractions and interfaces, pushing more of the execution on chain, and modernizing some of the wire formats. And all of this, you know, enhances resiliency, but it also allows us to move quicker and be more agile and deploy things and evolve the protocol more quickly,” Watt stated.

Second is Market Structure, which centers on Alpenglow, which aims for faster block distribution, and Constellation, which aims for clearer ordering rules and more competition among validators.

“Several important Alpenglow extensions are coming,” Watt stated. Alpenglow rolls out in two phases: first is Votor, its voting protocol, which is already live on the platform; second is Rotor, a single relay layer planned for a later release that will replace Turbine, the protocol that spreads a block’s data across the network.

Third is Performance, where network compute capacity doubles and transactions use 80% fewer compute units for token accounts. Last is Expressivity, which involves vector processing for models running fully onchain and an increase from 64 to 96 accounts per transaction.

Watt also spoke about improvements in onchain development: “The cost of storing data on Solana came down by 27% this year. And just in the coming two weeks, we're going to bring this thing down by another 7x.”

#5253. 178 Websites Infected in Major Optimizely Hack: Crypto Wallets Targeted, but Bitcoin Barely Reacted

Optimizely attack infects 178 websites, steals crypto and card data, and exposes users to wallet-address swaps and iPhone exploits.

An Optimizely attack on Monday, November 16, planted crypto-stealing code on the websites of 178 organizations, including Ledger, HSBC, Zoom, the BBC and CNN. The malicious script swapped crypto wallet addresses, skimmed card numbers, and tried to break into iPhones for about 19 hours before it was cleaned up.

BREAKING: A cyberattack hit 178 major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, BBC, Fox News, HSBC, Ledger, Equifax, Salesforce, IKEA and Air France-KLM, by loading malware on the Optimizely Web platform, exposing visitors to scripts built to steal payment data and exploit iOS…

— The Hormuz Letter (@HormuzLetter) November 17, 2026

Optimizely is a tool companies use to test different versions of their web pages. An attacker slipped code into the scripts it serves, so every site that loaded them ran the malware.

We traced the attacker’s Bitcoin wallet. It received five payments worth about $5,500, and one victim alone sent nearly 90% of it. Bitcoin barely moved while the attack ran.

So what happened, and what is the real impact of hacks like this one?

Security researcher Scott Helme of Report URI found the code and published a full breakdown. The attacker wrote it into a settings field in customers’ Optimizely projects, so it was served from Optimizely’s own servers and looked legitimate.

Optimizely said it “secured affected user accounts and added protections against further unauthorized code delivery.” Report URI found no sign that Ledger hardware wallets themselves were breached. The danger was on the website, where a copied address could be swapped before a user pasted it.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Security Analyst Recommends Best Anonymous Crypto Wallets

Report URI listed the attacker’s wallets. We checked the Bitcoin one on mempool.space, the public Bitcoin block explorer.

The Optimizely attack’s impact was tiny, and the market ignored it. Bitcoin is near $64,300 after its weekend low of $62,006, and that slide came from wider selling, not this attack.

EXPLORE: Crypto Hack Losses Hit $8.74 Billion in 2026, More Than Triple 2025: How Did Bitcoin and Ether React?

The money stolen in the Optimizely attack is small, but the method is the year’s most damaging one. We sorted DefiLlama’s 2026 hack list by attack type. Attacks on websites and infrastructure, rather than on smart contracts, are now the costliest category:

These attacks hit users where no wallet setting can protect them. The fix is on the user’s side: check the address on the hardware wallet’s screen before signing, send a small test transfer first, and keep phones updated.

On the daily chart, Bitcoin trades at $64,326. It sits below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $76,208, and its 200-day EMA at $75,864.

The Optimizely attack did not move Bitcoin, and the attacker walked away with about $7,000. Its real cost is trust: when a hardware-wallet maker’s own website can serve malware for hours, checking every address on the device is no longer optional.

#5252. XRP and Solana ETF Plans Abruptly Scrapped After Yearlong Wait

Investment firm Roundhill has suddenly terminated plans to launch two new XRP- and Solana (SOL)-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

This decision comes after over a year of regulatory filings and multiple delays.

As per the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings on Nov. 18, Roundhill has officially withdrawn plans to launch the Roundhill XRP Covered Call Strategy ETF and Roundhill Solana Covered Call Strategy ETF.

Interestingly, it submitted the applications for these two funds on Oct. 17, 2025. Therefore, these two funds had been awaiting launch for over 13 months.

As per the latest regulatory filings, Roundhill has been consistently delaying the effective dates for these two funds.

However, instead of launching them, the investment firm has decided to drop both products.

In its requests to withdraw the filings for these funds, Roundhill revealed that it "has no further intention to pursue effectiveness of the Fund." The firm noted that it had not sold any shares under the registrations for these two funds.

Intriguingly, Roundhill failed to elaborate on the sudden decision to axe its plans to launch these two ETFs.

Roundhill was planning to launch income-generating XRP and Solana ETFs using a covered call strategy. In such a strategy, investors sell options to earn premiums while also maintaining exposure to the price movements of XRP and Solana.

Unlike spot-based ETFs, these funds would not have held the cryptocurrencies directly. Instead, they would have used options written against existing cryptocurrency ETFs.

A covered call strategy can be useful for generating regular income. However, it can also cap profits during strong market rallies.

Notably, there has been relatively low demand for income-generating cryptocurrency investment products. This raises concerns about investors' interest in these ETFs.

Surprisingly, this decision came amid substantial net inflows into spot-based XRP and Solana ETFs.

U.S. spot XRP and Solana ETFs recorded net inflows of roughly $969 million between May and October 2026, according to data from SoSoValue.

Overall, these spot ETFs held around $3.26 billion in assets under management as of the end of October.

#5251. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor announced gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Users who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

The gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

Gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example shows the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

The limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is announced, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

The docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

That makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

Bitcoin price crashes below $58,000, hitting its lowest level since September 2024 as the crypto sell-off accelerates.

BTC faces its seventh consecutive weekly loss, marking its longest losing streak since 2022 as institutional demand weakens.

ETF outflows, tech-stock weakness and liquidations intensify selling pressure, putting $50,000 back on traders' radar.

Bitcoin’s sell-off has entered a critical phase after BTC plunged below $58,000, extending its decline to levels last seen in September 2024. The cryptocurrency has fallen sharply from its record high, while persistent selling threatens to extend its weekly losing streak to seven weeks.

The breakdown is coinciding with a broader retreat from risk assets, heavy Bitcoin ETF withdrawals and mounting concerns over technology-stock valuations. With several major support levels now broken, investors are increasingly watching whether Bitcoin price can stabilize or whether the next leg of the correction could take prices toward $50,000.

Bitcoin’s latest decline reflects a broader deterioration in risk appetite across financial markets. A sharp sell-off in AI and technology stocks has triggered investors to reduce exposure to volatile assets, with cryptocurrencies facing additional pressure from institutional withdrawals and leveraged liquidations.

The institutional demand picture has also weakened significantly. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $582 million in net outflows in a single session, while BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for around $541 million of the withdrawals. November ETF outflows have approached $3.5 billion, removing a major source of buying support from the market.

Meanwhile, falling prices have triggered liquidations of leveraged positions, accelerating Bitcoin’s downward momentum. The combination of ETF redemptions, weaker equity markets and forced selling has created a difficult environment for BTC bulls.

Bitcoin’s daily chart shows a decisive breakdown from its previous consolidation range. BTC initially lost support around the $75,000 region before accelerating lower through the $68,000–$64,000 zone. The subsequent breakdown below $60,000 further weakened the technical structure.

The latest move below $58,000 leaves Bitcoin trading near a critical support region, with the $50,000 level emerging as the next major downside target if selling pressure continues. Bitcoin’s ability to reclaim $60,000 could provide short-term relief. However, a broader recovery would require BTC to regain previously broken support zones and attract renewed buying demand.

The $50,000 level is increasingly entering the market conversation as Bitcoin loses support and momentum remains bearish. A sustained breakdown below the current support region could expose BTC to further downside, particularly if ETF outflows continue and global risk sentiment deteriorates.

However, an extended sell-off could also create conditions for a sharp relief rally as short positions increase and investors begin looking for value at lower prices. For now, Bitcoin’s immediate direction depends on whether buyers defend the $55,000–$58,000 region or selling pressure pushes BTC toward $50,000. Until key resistance levels are reclaimed, the technical outlook remains tilted toward the downside.

Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin led the daily ranking of stablecoin inflows into decentralized finance (DeFi), according to Token Terminal data that RWA Foundation shared on X. The DeFi total value locked (TVL) of Ripple's stablecoin grew by $22.3 million over 24 hours, and Tether added $21.6 million. RWA Foundation titled its chart "Ripple led stablecoin DeFi growth."

Paxos, Open Standard and Societe Generale followed with $7.8 million, $4 million and $1.2 million, respectively. World Liberty, United Stables, MetaMask, Tori and Liquity each added less than $700,000 over the same period.

About $2.8 billion worth of RLUSD is in circulation, compared with about $180 billion worth of Tether's USDT. Tether's stablecoin is still more than 60 times bigger than RLUSD.

Ripple launched RLUSD in December 2024. In mid-September 2026, RLUSD supply passed $2.44 billion, and about $1.38 billion of it was on Ethereum. About $1.05 billion was on the XRP Ledger, Ripple's home network. On Ethereum, the stablecoin is used in DeFi pools on Aave V3, Curve and Morpho.

RLUSD is issued by Standard Custody & Trust under the supervision of the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS), and its reserves are held at custodian bank BNY. Ripple has also integrated RLUSD with payment providers Arf, Convera and Cross River Bank, and the stablecoin is now used in dollar settlements between companies.

#5245. Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16. Here is how the nine tracks, the 1,000 ENJ deposit and conviction voting work, and what the Relaychain vote shows.

Enjin's new proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ. It's actually the cheap part.

Enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release. The referendum opened November 10. If it passes, the upgrade is targeted for November 16 at block #12,319,600, with the network moving from runtime 1.3.1 to 1.4.3. Enjin's Fort Canning announcement lays out the plan, and the official changelog carries the technical detail.

The Relaychain has already made the jump. Referendum #16 approved its upgrade on October 28, and it went live on November 9. The Matrixchain vote is the second half of one upgrade, and it is the half that changes how Matrixchain makes decisions from then on.

Early coverage reported the schedule and the headline numbers: nine tracks, 1,000 ENJ. The changelog and the governance portal show the mechanics behind them, and those mechanics change more than the headlines suggest.

Today, the Matrixchain runs its governance through the older Democracy, Council and Technical Committee pallets, the modules that handle proposals and votes. Fort Canning replaces all three with a new set: Referenda, Conviction Voting, Origins, Whitelist and the Enjin Fellowship. Under OpenGov, any account can submit a referendum on one of nine tracks, and from the moment the upgrade lands, Matrixchain's own upgrades go through that process.

A track is a lane for a particular kind of decision. Enjin's changelog describes the families: Root and the admin tracks for the highest-stakes changes, Whitelisted Caller for proposals the Fellowship fast-tracks, and two special tracks, Referendum Killer and Referendum Canceller, for stopping a proposal that shouldn't proceed. Matrixchain gets no treasury tracks: those, sized by how much a proposal would spend, stay on the Relaychain, where treasury requests now go. Each track has its own deposit, approval curve and enactment period, and the Enjin Fellowship can fast-track time-sensitive proposals.

Splitting decisions this way means a small treasury request doesn't face the same bar as a change to the chain's core. Riskier tracks demand larger deposits and more support, while smaller ones move faster and cost less.

The submission deposit rises from 0.025 ENJ to 1,000 ENJ on every track, a 40,000-fold increase. The deposit is refunded when a referendum passes or is canceled, and it exists to deter spam. As an illustration, using the roughly $66 million market cap reported in early October, ENJ traded near three cents, which would put 1,000 ENJ around $33.

That is only the entry ticket. The cost that matters comes next. A referendum also needs a decision deposit before it moves into voting, and the changelog lists steep figures: 2,500,000 ENJ on Root and Fellowship Admin, 1,000,000 ENJ on the other admin tracks, and 2,500 to 250,000 ENJ on the Relaychain's treasury tracks. At the same illustrative price, the 2.5 million ENJ Root deposit comes to roughly $80,000, about 0.12% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance.

So proposing is cheap, and pushing a proposal through is not. Anyone can raise an idea, but anyone who wants the network to vote on something big needs real stake in the outcome. The changelog says the same values apply on both chains, and Matrixchain adopts them for its new tracks.

The best evidence of how these votes work comes from the Relaychain referendum that has already finished. Enjin's governance portal shows referendum #16 as finalised, approved on October 28 and enacted on November 9.

The final tally on the page is small. Eleven voters cast 381,303.02 ENJ of conviction-weighted voting power, and all of it went to Aye: 100% in favor, 0 ENJ against. The page also shows raw, unweighted support of 271,303.2 ENJ, which it describes as the total balance backing the proposal and the figure the support curve uses. The conviction multiplier on the page runs from under 1x up to 6x.

Two numbers stand out. First, an entire chain upgrade passed with 271,303 ENJ of raw support, about 0.013% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance, a figure worked out from the portal's number. Second, conviction added about 110,000 ENJ of weight on top of the raw balance, an average multiplier of roughly 1.4x. Voters picked up some extra weight, but most didn't lock their tokens for the long periods that earn the top multipliers.

A 100% Aye result says little by itself. A scheduled upgrade with no organized opposition passes easily, and the tally shows how thin engagement was.

Fort Canning adds the safeguard that thin turnout calls for. A referendum now needs a minimum share of total ENJ voting in support. The changelog sets 0.5% on Root and the admin tracks, 0.005% to 0.125% on the Relaychain's treasury tracks, 0.1% for Referendum Killer and 0.05% for Referendum Canceller. Measured against 2.02 billion ENJ, that means about 10.1 million ENJ on Root, roughly 101,000 to 2.5 million on the treasury tracks, about 2.02 million to kill a referendum and about 1.01 million to cancel one.

Referendum #16's 271,303 ENJ of raw support would clear the lowest treasury floor of about 101,000 ENJ, but it would miss the Root floor by a factor of about 37. The page doesn't show which track the referendum used, and a runtime upgrade typically sits on a high-stakes track, so the Root comparison works as an illustration and not as a finding. The floors also didn't exist when #16 passed, since Fort Canning introduced them.

That is the real change. Under the new rules, 11 wallets can't carry a chain-level decision on their own. Low turnout means failure, and proposals that matter will need far more ENJ behind them. Enjin's changelog says Matrixchain upgrades go through OpenGov starting with this one, which suggests today's vote still runs on the current system, so the floors will first bite on the first OpenGov referendum.

Holders who haven't voted can still do so through Enjin's governance portal before the window closes. Voting locks tokens, so the lock length is worth checking first. Enjin's support article on voting explains the trade-off: the longer the lock, the more a vote counts, and tokens stay locked until the period ends.

Node operators on the Matrixchain can wait for the result before upgrading, as Enjin has indicated, and then follow the changelog for the version to install. Relaychain operators already needed client version 1.8.1.

This vote is more about control than speed. OpenGov spreads decisions across tracks with deposits and support floors built for the weight of each choice, and it moves ENJ holders from voting on a handful of items to a standing governance system. The Relaychain's first vote showed how little participation it took under the old rules, and the first referenda after November 16 will show whether holders turn out for the new ones. If most proposals stall at the decision deposit, the system costs too much. If they clear with a handful of voters, the floors aren't doing their job. Either result will tell holders what their ENJ can do.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 2.36% over the past 24 hours and was trading at $0.00000389 on Nov. 19, close to its lowest level of the year. Earlier this month, the meme coin set a new yearly low of $0.00000373, according to TradingView data. SHIB is now heading into December, and CryptoRank data shows that December has been the worst month for the token so far.

SHIB's median return in December is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank. November comes next, with a median return of -16.4%.

#5240. NEAR’s Inflation Cut: The Math Behind a 5.27% to 3.37% Staking Yield

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

HSP-029 lowers NEAR’s issuance cap from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. The cap formula, the epoch step and the yield math show what that does to stakers.

Most headlines on NEAR’s new inflation schedule stop at “2.5% to 1.6%.” Stakers feel a different number. They earn about 5.27% today and will earn roughly 3.37% once the cut finishes, and a single line of arithmetic accounts for the gap.

House of Stake ratified HSP-029 on November 16, after the Security Council’s 14-day veto window passed without a veto. The proposal touches one parameter, the maximum annual issuance rate, which drops from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. It is the second cut in just over a year, coming after the October 2025 halving from 5%.

Everything else stays put. Issuance still splits 90% to staking participants and 10% to the protocol treasury. There is no new spending program, no validator subsidy and no automatic trigger that could push issuance back up. The full proposal models 11.8 million NEAR of issuance avoided over two years and 66.1 million over six, measured against leaving the cap at 2.5%.

The schedule is a straight line with no stair steps:

Here t is the number of months since the reduction begins. The 0.9% is the total drop (2.5 minus 1.6), and dividing it by 24 gives a monthly step of 0.0375 percentage points, or 3.75 basis points. The min(t, 24) term caps the ramp at month 24, and the cap sits at 1.6% from there on.

NEAR applies the step every epoch rather than once a month. An epoch lasts about 12 hours, so the cap slips by roughly 0.0006 percentage points each time, far too little to notice on any given day. There are no step dates to mark on a calendar. Sampled every six months, the line looks like this:

The yield column uses the math in the next section. It drops about 0.08 percentage points a month, evenly, with no cliff.

New tokens go mostly to stakers, so the staked pool splits the reward, and a smaller pool earns more per token. That gives a working formula:

gross yield ≈ 0.9 × issuance cap ÷ staking ratio

The 0.9 is the staker share of issuance. Using the proposal’s figures, 0.9 × 2.5% ÷ 0.4271 comes to 5.27%, where 42.71% is the staking ratio reported when the proposal went to vote. Put in the 1.6% cap and 0.9 × 1.6% ÷ 0.4271 gives 3.37%, the same number the proposal publishes. Anyone can check the headline yields on a calculator.

The formula has two limits. It uses the cap, but realized issuance runs a little lower because transaction fees are burned. HSP-029 measured 2.45% in September, which puts today’s yield near 5.16%. The staking ratio also moves. When more people stake, the same rewards spread over more tokens and yield falls further, and when people unstake it climbs. The 3.37% figure assumes today’s ratio holds.

Stakers feel it first. By the proposal’s own math, someone staking 1,000 NEAR ends up with about 20 fewer tokens after two years than if the cap had stayed at 2.5%. The numbers back that up: yield averages about 4.32% across the ramp, roughly 0.95 points under today’s rate for two years.

Holders who don’t stake come out ahead. More than half of NEAR’s supply sits unstaked, and every new token dilutes those holdings. Trimming the cap by 0.9 percentage points trims that dilution by the same amount each year. Stakers give up some reward so that everyone else gives up less value.

Validators get an easier path than in 2025, when the halving cut staking rewards from about 9% to 4.75% in a single upgrade. Operators now have 24 months to plan. NEAR’s analysis finds that most validator revenue comes from commission on delegated stake, so service quality and fee competition shape income more than the issuance rate does.

Recent history explains the setup. When the 2025 halving shipped, an earlier community poll had missed the two-thirds threshold, and critics said the core team pushed the change through anyway. HSP-029 sidesteps that argument by design.

Two separate approvals are required. Token holders voting through veNEAR set the direction, and that vote closed November 2 with 99.96% in favor and none against. Validators then decide on their own whether to adopt the protocol upgrade that makes the cap binding. The author, Sal Ternullo of SVRN, opened discussion on October 7, and the process ran through the Screening Committee and Security Council in public. Raising issuance again would take a new proposal and another round of validator adoption, so nothing can be added quietly later.

Ratification does not change issuance yet. A one-quarter grace period comes first, giving wallets, exchanges, custodians and staking providers time to update their disclosures. NEAR One then releases the upgrade and validators choose whether to adopt it, with the reduction starting about a quarter after ratification. On schedule, that means a start in early 2027 and a 1.6% cap around early 2029.

Three things are worth tracking. Validator adoption of the upgrade comes first, because the cap stays at 2.5% until enough validators run it. The staking ratio comes next, since it moves yield regardless of the formula. Last are the quarterly transparency reports NEAR has promised, which compare realized issuance with the schedule.

Price is a separate question. Lower issuance eases supply pressure, but nothing in it creates demand. The cap will follow its published line down, and yield will follow the cap.

Stock market crash fears intensify as Nasdaq plunges 10% and S&P 500 drops 8.6% in its worst week since April 2025.

Dow and S&P 500 enter correction territory, falling more than 10% from their record highs as Wall Street's sell-off accelerates.

AI and semiconductor stocks lead the crash, with Nvidia, AMD, Micron and other technology stocks facing heavy losses.

The US stock market crash intensified this week as investors aggressively dumped technology and artificial intelligence stocks, pushing major Wall Street indexes toward their steepest weekly declines in years. The Nasdaq Composite plunged approximately 10%, marking its worst week since the March 2020 pandemic crash, while the S&P 500 lost 8.6%.

Both the S&P 500 and Dow Jones entered correction territory, raising concerns that the AI-driven market rally may be facing a deeper repricing.

With technology stocks leading the decline, investors are now questioning whether the latest stock market crash signals a temporary correction or the beginning of a broader downturn.

Wall Street’s losses accelerated on Friday, with major indexes closing sharply lower after another wave of selling hit AI and semiconductor stocks.

On Friday, the S&P 500 fell 3.7% to close at 6,910.39, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 949 points, closing at 48,147.33.

This is the WORST WEEK for the STOCK MARKET since March 2020Nasdaq 100: -5.6% today, -10.4% this week, worst since 2020.S&P 500: -3.7% today, -8.6% this week, its worst week since April 2025Semiconductors: -10.7% today, -17.1% this week, worst since 2001 pic.twitter.com/2Z9gqG5Ype

The S&P 500 and Dow are now more than 10% below their recent record highs, confirming corrections in both indexes. The Nasdaq has also erased its gains for 2026.

The latest stock market crash is primarily driven by growing concerns surrounding the artificial intelligence trade. Investors have poured enormous capital into AI infrastructure, chipmakers and data-center companies.

However, rising valuations and uncertainty over whether AI investments can generate sufficient returns are prompting investors to reassess the sector’s growth expectations. The sell-off intensified following the market’s reaction to Anthropic’s public debut, which failed to restore confidence in AI stocks. Investors also remain concerned about interest rates, inflation and the possibility of tighter monetary conditions.

The result has been a sharp unwinding of crowded technology trades, with losses spreading beyond individual AI companies into the broader stock market.

Semiconductor stocks have suffered the most severe losses as investors reduce exposure to AI-related companies. Nvidia fell approximately 23% for the week, marking its worst weekly performance since 2008. AMD lost around 20.5%, while Micron and other chipmakers also faced significant selling pressure.

The semiconductor sector’s 17.1% weekly decline highlights the scale of the repricing underway in the AI trade. Companies that previously drove Wall Street’s rally are now becoming the biggest contributors to the market’s losses

The immediate outlook for Wall Street remains uncertain. The latest correction has raised concerns about valuations, AI spending and investor positioning, but a correction does not automatically signal a prolonged bear market.

Investors will closely watch whether technology stocks stabilize, whether volatility eases and whether companies can deliver earnings growth strong enough to justify their valuations. For now, the stock market crash has exposed the risks of Wall Street’s heavy dependence on AI stocks.

If selling continues across semiconductor and technology companies, the broader market could remain under pressure heading into the next trading week.

Chainflip lost nearly $4.86 million after an attacker drained its Ethereum vault.

he exploit targeted Chainflip’s cryptographic signing system rather than a smart contract bug.

The latest incident marks Chainflip’s second major security breach in just over two months.

Chainflip, a decentralized cross-chain swap protocol, has faced another security scare after nearly $4.86 million in crypto was drained from its Ethereum vault in a single transaction. The attacker moved the stolen funds through Tornado Cash within just nine minutes, forcing the protocol to halt deposits, withdrawals, and swaps.

While its team investigates how the funds were taken.

On-chain investigations by Bitquery show that the attacker targeted Chainflip’s cryptographic key system rather than exploiting a bug in its smart contracts.

The attacker first obtained a valid Schnorr signature from the Ethereum Vault’s Threshold Signature Scheme (TSS) aggregate key. This allowed the attacker to pass the vault’s normal signature checks.

On November 21, 2026, a newly funded wallet (0x78fa) called the Vault.transferBatch function. The transaction passed verification and drained all the vault’s available funds in a single move.

The attacker then moved quickly to hide the stolen funds. Within nine minutes, the exploiter swapped the 3,249,631.41 USDC and 758,141.33 USDT for 2,909 ETH (worth around $4.86 million), then sent it to Tornado Cash in 38 separate batches.

Chainflip has not yet confirmed the $4.86 million loss. Instead, the protocol said it was aware of a potential exploit affecting its vaults and moved into full safe mode as a precaution.

We’re aware of a potential exploit affecting Chainflip vaults.As a precaution, the protocol is being put into full safe mode. Deposits, withdrawals, swaps and quoting are disabled.We’re investigating and will share updates here as we learn more.

“Deposits, withdrawals, swaps, and quoting are disabled; we’re investigating and will share updates here as we learn more.”

This is Chainflip’s second major attack in just over two months. On September 12, 2026, the protocol lost $736,442 in a separate exploit targeting its TRON integration. That attack was caused by a software flaw in how Chainflip processed TRON transaction data, while the November 21 attack targeted its Ethereum Vault’s cryptographic signing key.

After the September attack, Chainflip paused TRON swaps and used its surplus reserves to fully reimburse affected liquidity providers in USDC.

The protocol has yet to confirm whether it will follow the same recovery plan for the latest $4.86 million loss.

#5235. Popular Commentator Slams Cardano as a ‘Largely Failed Blockchain’ as Solana Leaves ADA in the Dust on Adoption Metrics

Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano is facing fresh criticism for struggling to attract users and generate on-chain activity, despite being nearly nine years into its development.

Widely-followed crypto analyst Lark Davis has branded the network a “largely failed blockchain,” pointing to a stark adoption gap with Solana, which launched four years later but has significantly outpaced ADA in daily users, perpetual futures trading volume, and application revenue.

Despite having nearly a decade to establish itself in the blockchain industry, Cardano continues to face questions about its ability to attract users and generate meaningful network activity. Analyst Lark Davis has commented on the adoption gap between Cardano and Solana, arguing that Solana has significantly outperformed ADA despite launching four years later.

“Nine years in and Cardano is still waiting on adoption,” Davis wrote on X.

According to Davis, Cardano accounts for just around 1% of Solana’s daily users, highlighting the stark difference in activity between the two networks. The gap reportedly extends beyond user numbers, with Cardano recording only about 0.3% of Solana’s perpetual futures trading volume.

The revenue figures paint an even more challenging picture for the Cardano ecosystem. Davis estimates that Cardano generates roughly 0.2% of the application revenue recorded across Solana’s ecosystem, further highlighting the difference in economic activity between the competing networks.

Based on these figures, Davis delivered a particularly harsh assessment of Cardano, describing it as a “largely failed blockchain.” His criticism centers on the contrast between Cardano’s nine-year journey and Solana’s ability to build a considerably larger user base and generate more trading activity and application revenue in a shorter period.

The latest criticism follows a series of similar remarks from Davis about Cardano’s adoption challenges. As ZyCrypto previously reported, the analyst had also taken aim at Cardano over its relatively small user base, questioning the network’s ability to attract and retain users despite years of development.

Despite his harsh assessment of Cardano’s fundamentals, Davis has occasionally expressed optimism about ADA’s price prospects.

In November 2025, for instance, he suggested that Cardano could stage a rally similar to XRP’s 2024 surge, pointing to the strength of its community and brand as potential catalysts.

More recently, on September 28, Davis argued that Cardano’s “cult following” could help drive ADA back toward $1, with further upside potentially taking the token to $1.50 or even $2.

However, these bullish price projections focused more on speculative market demand and Cardano’s dedicated community than on measurable improvements in network adoption or ecosystem activity.

Gold (XAU) fell 2.5% to about $3,770 an ounce on Wednesday, November 18, as traders bet on a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Silver dropped 3.3% to $45.70. Both metals are at their lowest since September 2025. The BTC price held near $64,600, but it has fallen even harder than the metals since the hike bets took off.

Gold prices sink beneath $3,800, hitting a 14-month low as the hawkish Fed outlook and firm dollar weigh on bullion – FX

— First Squawk (@FirstSquawk) November 18, 2026

We compared the moves since November 5, the day before a strong October jobs report changed the rate outlook. Bitcoin is down 15%, silver 12.5% and gold 8.4%. Over the same days, the U.S. dollar index rose 2.2%, and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed from 4.84% to 5.10%.

Higher rates hit everything that pays no interest, and gold, silver and bitcoin all fall into that group. So the next big test is the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting.

Gold peaked near $5,320 an ounce on COMEX futures in late January. It has since lost 29%, and silver has lost 60% from its January high of $115. On Monday, gold for immediate delivery touched $3,832, and Wednesday’s drop pushed it lower still.

The reason is the Fed. Markets now treat another hike as almost certain:

A quarter-point hike would lift the Fed’s target range to 4.00%-4.25%. It would be the second this year, after September’s. Waller has gone further, saying a half-point move, or “a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered.”

Central banks are still buying gold, 675 tonnes in the first nine months of the year. That hasn’t been enough to offset a stronger dollar and higher yields.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best Low-Cap Crypto

Some investors call bitcoin “digital gold,” but in this selloff the BTC price hasn’t acted as a hedge.

We matched daily moves over the last 15 gold trading sessions, from October 29 to November 18:

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index sits at 11, deep in “extreme fear,” just above the weekend’s low of 10.

EXPLORE: Bank of America Warns of 50 bps Fed Hike in December: Is Bitcoin Heading for Another 2022-Style Drop?

With a quarter-point hike at 95%, that move is largely expected already. For the BTC price, the surprise would be a bigger move or a pause:

The minutes of the October meeting come out today at 2 p.m. ET and could move the odds before December. In October, two officials, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, voted to hike when the rest voted to hold.

The BTC price stands at $64,590 on Binance, down 48% from its October 2025 record. On the daily chart, it sits below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $75,780, and its 200-day EMA at $75,760.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Reveals Upcoming Binance Listings

Gold, silver and bitcoin are all trading as bets on the Fed right now. Until December 9, the BTC price is likely to keep moving with yields and the dollar, not against them.

Bitcoin (BTC) price continues to fall as the sell-off from the $86,000 - $87,000 region in October is gathering momentum. The sell-off has accelerated in recent days, and BTC price has slipped to roughly $61,900, moving closer to the next technical support level at $60,000.

The daily chart shows several concerning technical developments for Bitcoin. Shorter-term moving averages continue to fall below longer-term moving averages, forming a technical pattern commonly known as a death cross. The death cross has now formed twice with 100 and 200 EMAs, indicating a worsening technical setup for Bitcoin, commonly known as a double death cross.

Several key moving averages continue to cluster in the $75,000 - $76,000 region, adding resistance for Bitcoin price action.

Relative Strength Index (RSI) has started to move closer to the oversold region, indicating that momentum has started to slow for Bitcoin.

Taken together, this technical setup indicates that selling pressure for Bitcoin has been increasing on multiple time frames. We are monitoring $60,000 as a key support level. This level was also an area of interest for buyers during the June correction in Bitcoin.

Should BTC price continue to move lower and break out below $60,000, the next level of support to watch will be $58,000, followed by $56,000.

For Bitcoin price to reverse course and show signs of a meaningful short-term rebound, it will need to continue higher and break out above $64,000 - $65,000.

Breaking out above $68,000 would be a strong move that could help to stabilize Bitcoin in the short term. A positive move for Bitcoin would need to continue higher and reclaim several key moving averages. Until then, Bitcoin will continue to trade in a more bearish technical setup.

Bitcoin price action continues to move lower on the daily chart. All technical indicators on this chart continue to deteriorate, indicating that Bitcoin remains vulnerable to another leg lower before buyers can show signs of a robust short-term recovery.
